title: Physics — Unit 2 Forces of Earth (targets 2.1-2.3)
source: Carter's three learning-target pages for Unit 2 (2.1 interior processes, 2.2 geological cause and effect, 2.3 geologic time), rebuilt as 33 items with equal-word-count options so length cannot hint at the answer.

questions.stem: A cross-section model has to show which layer is liquid. Which claim is correct, and what is the evidence?
options: Outer core; shear waves stop at this boundary
Mantle; it flows slowly under the rigid plates
Inner core; it is hotter than layers above
Crust; it bends plastically beneath the deep oceans
questions.why: Only the outer core is liquid, and S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, which is the seismic evidence.

questions.stem: The inner core is hotter than the outer core, yet it is solid. Why?
options: Iron becomes solid as it loses radiogenic heat
Pressure at that depth raises the melting point
Inner core is actually cooler than the mantle
Convection in the core removes heat very quickly
questions.why: Melting point rises with pressure, so the deepest iron stays solid despite a temperature above the outer core's.

questions.stem: A student writes that the mantle is molten rock. Which correction is right?
options: The mantle is liquid only beneath the deep oceans
The mantle is solid and never deforms at all
The mantle is solid rock that flows over time
The mantle is a gas at those asthenosphere depths
questions.why: The mantle is solid; it deforms plastically over geologic time, and only the outer core is liquid.

questions.stem: Where inside Earth do nuclear processes occur, and which process is it?
options: Crust only; fusion of hydrogen into helium gas
Core only; fusion of iron into heavier nuclei
Mantle only; fission of silicate minerals into oxides
Core and mantle; radioactive decay of heavy isotopes
questions.why: Long-lived isotopes such as U-238, U-235, Th-232 and K-40 decay in the core and mantle; fusion is a stellar process.

questions.stem: How does one radioactive decay event deliver heat to the surrounding rock?
options: Emitted particles and gamma rays are absorbed
The nucleus releases chemical bonds that burn
Friction between decaying atoms generates the heat
Magnetic reconnection converts each decay into photons
questions.why: Decay energy leaves as particle kinetic energy and gamma radiation, which the surrounding rock absorbs and thermalizes.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes the two sources of Earth's internal heat?
options: Primordial is continuous; radiogenic is leftover heat
Primordial is leftover; radiogenic is produced continuously
Primordial is solar; radiogenic comes from friction
Primordial is tidal; radiogenic comes from pressure
questions.why: Primordial heat is accretional heat still draining out; radiogenic heat is generated now by radioactive decay.

questions.stem: If radiogenic heating declined sharply, what would happen to plate motion?
options: Convection would strengthen and plates would speed
Convection would reverse and plates would stop
Convection would weaken and plates would slow
Convection stops although plates continue moving quickly
questions.why: Decay heat sustains convection; less heat means weaker convection, less slab pull, and slower plates.

questions.stem: Why does hot mantle material rise in a convection cell?
options: It is pushed upward by the overriding plate above
It is denser than the material beneath the crust
It is pulled upward by the nearby sinking slab
It is less dense than the surrounding cooler rock
questions.why: Rising material is buoyant because it is less dense; nothing needs to push it up.

questions.stem: On a force vector diagram of a plate, which arrow should be drawn largest?
options: Slab pull at the subducting end, pointing downward
Ridge push at the spreading end, pointing outward
Friction along the plate base, opposing its motion
Mantle drag along the base, following the flow
questions.why: Slab pull is the dominant plate force, so its vector should be longest and labeled.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly connects convection to a force acting on a plate?
options: Rising hot rock pushes the plate away from ridges
Sinking cool rock drags the plate toward the trench
Spreading ridges pull the plate toward the nearby continent
Mantle drag pushes the plate upward into the crust
questions.why: The descending limb drags lithosphere down and inward, which is the mechanism behind slab pull.

questions.stem: At a divergent boundary in an ocean basin, which feature forms?
options: A deep trench with deep earthquakes and island arcs
A strike-slip fault with shallow quakes and no magma
A mid-ocean ridge with shallow earthquakes and active volcanism
A folded mountain belt made of thickened continental crust
questions.why: Divergence creates new oceanic crust at a ridge, with shallow quakes and decompression melting.

questions.stem: An oceanic plate meets a continental plate. What forms, and why?
options: Folded mountains and no trench, because neither plate subducts
A ridge and rift valley, because plates move apart
A transform fault, because the plates slide past sideways
Trench and volcanic arc, because the oceanic plate subducts
questions.why: Oceanic lithosphere is denser, so it subducts, producing a trench and a volcanic arc above the slab.

questions.stem: Two continental plates collide. What is the result?
options: A folded mountain belt with thickened crust, no trench
A trench with deep earthquakes and explosive arc volcanoes
A mid-ocean ridge with new crust and shallow quakes
A transform fault with offset streams and no volcanism
questions.why: Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct, so the plates shorten and thicken into a mountain belt.

questions.stem: Which set of features belongs to a transform boundary?
options: Deep earthquakes, island arcs, and explosive volcanism
Shallow earthquakes, offset stream channels, no volcanism
Shallow earthquakes, new oceanic crust, and ridges
Intermediate earthquakes, folded rock, and thick crust
questions.why: Transform motion is strike-slip: shallow quakes, offset features, and no magma because nothing rises or sinks.

questions.stem: Earthquake depth increases with distance from a trench. What does that show?
options: Quakes follow the hot mantle as it rises
Quakes follow the ridge as new crust forms
Quakes follow the cold slab as it sinks
Quakes follow the fault as plates slide sideways
questions.why: The Benioff zone tracks the dipping slab, which is why deep quakes occur only at subduction zones.

questions.stem: Why does a transform boundary produce no volcanoes?
options: Magma forms there but cannot reach the surface very quickly
The crust is too thin to hold a magma chamber
The plates there move too slowly to generate any heat
No material rises or subducts there, so nothing ever melts
questions.why: Melting needs decompression or added water; transform motion supplies neither, so no magma is generated.

questions.stem: Magnetic striping on the seafloor is symmetric about a ridge. What does it prove?
options: New crust records field reversals as it spreads outward
Old crust is folded by compression at the ridge
The ridge moves sideways across a stationary ocean floor
Deep sediment layers align with the present magnetic field
questions.why: Basalt records the field as it cools, and the mirrored pattern on both sides shows crust moving away from the ridge.

questions.stem: Ocean crust is nowhere older than about 200 million years. Why?
options: Ocean crust forms too slowly to accumulate older rock
Ocean crust is recycled into trenches at subduction zones
The ocean crust is continually melted by ridge volcanism
Ocean crust is buried by sediment before aging further
questions.why: Oceanic lithosphere is destroyed at subduction zones, so the oldest seafloor is far younger than the continents.

questions.stem: Heat flow is high at a ridge and low far from it. What explains the pattern?
options: Old crust far from the ridge is heating up
Friction at the ridge generates heat along the fault
New crust near the ridge is hot and cooling
Thick sediment insulates the crust far from the ridge
questions.why: Crust cools and thickens with distance from the ridge, so heat flow falls as the lithosphere ages.

questions.stem: A GPS station moves 4 cm per year. How far does it travel in 25 million years?
options: 100 km, since 4 cm per year is 4 km per million
10,000 km, since 4 cm per year is 400 km per million
400 km, since 4 cm per year is 16 km per million
1,000 km, since 4 cm per year is 40 km per million
questions.why: 1 cm/yr equals 10 km per million years, so 4 cm/yr gives 40 km/My and 25 My gives 1,000 km.

questions.stem: How is a half-life defined for a radioactive isotope?
options: The time for half the parent atoms to decay
The time for all parent atoms to decay completely
The time for half the daughter atoms to escape
The time for the isotope to change its temperature
questions.why: A half-life is the interval in which half of the remaining parent decays, and it is constant for that isotope.

questions.stem: What fraction of the original parent remains after four half-lives?
options: 25 percent, because the parent halves only twice
6.25 percent, because the parent halves four times
12.5 percent, because the parent halves three times
3.125 percent, because the parent halves five times
questions.why: Each half-life halves the parent: 50, 25, 12.5, then 6.25 percent after four.

questions.stem: A sample holds 12.5 percent of its original parent isotope. How many half-lives have passed?
options: Two, because the parent halved two separate times
Four, because the parent halved four separate times
Three, because the parent halved three separate times
Five, because the parent halved five separate times
questions.why: 100 to 50 to 25 to 12.5 percent is three halvings, so n = 3.

questions.stem: A rock holds 12.5 percent parent and the isotope has a 700-million-year half-life. What is its age?
options: 1.4 billion years, because two half-lives have passed
2.8 billion years, because four half-lives have passed
700 million years, because one half-life has passed
2.1 billion years, because three half-lives have passed
questions.why: n = 3 and each half-life is 700 My, so age = 3 x 700 My = 2.1 billion years.

questions.stem: A sample shows a parent-to-daughter ratio of 1:3. How many half-lives have passed?
options: Two, because 75 percent of the parent has decayed
One, because 50 percent of the parent has decayed
Three, because 87.5 percent of the parent has decayed
Four, because 93.75 percent of the parent has decayed
questions.why: Daughter at 75 percent means parent at 25 percent, which is two halvings.

questions.stem: Why is carbon-14 unsuitable for dating a 70-million-year-old rock?
options: Its 1.25-billion-year half-life leaves too little daughter
Its 5,730-year half-life leaves too little parent
Its 4.5-billion-year half-life leaves too little parent
Its 48.8-billion-year half-life leaves too little daughter
questions.why: Beyond about ten half-lives the remaining parent is unmeasurable, and C-14 also dates only once-living material.

questions.stem: Which isotope would you use to date a volcanic ash layer, and why?
options: Carbon-14, because its half-life suits million-year rock
Uranium-238, because its half-life suits thousand-year bone
Potassium-40, because its half-life suits million-year rock
Rubidium-87, because its half-life suits thousand-year shell
questions.why: K-40 has a half-life near 1.25 billion years and is built into volcanic minerals, so it dates the eruption.

questions.stem: Which difference between relative and absolute dating is stated correctly?
options: Relative gives years; absolute gives only the relative order
Relative uses the radioactive isotopes; absolute uses rock superposition
Relative dates single minerals; absolute dates whole rock units
Relative gives order; absolute gives an age in years
questions.why: Relative dating orders events using superposition and cross-cutting; absolute dating converts a ratio into years.

questions.stem: A fault cuts through three sedimentary layers. What can you conclude?
options: The fault is younger than the layers it cuts
The fault is older than the layers it cuts
Fault is the same age as the lowest layer
The fault is older than the folded rock intrusion
questions.why: Cross-cutting relationships: a feature that cuts another must be younger than what it cuts.

questions.stem: How would you find the absolute age of a fossil between two ash layers?
options: Date the fossil bone itself directly with uranium-lead isotopes
Date both ash layers, bracketing the fossil between them
Date the sedimentary rock grains surrounding the whole fossil
Date the lowest layer in the exposed cliff section
questions.why: Volcanic ash is datable and bounds the fossil in time, which is why ash layers are the standard bracket.

questions.stem: Why does constant radioactive decay let geologists read a rock's age?
options: The decay rate slows predictably as the rock gets older
The daughter isotope leaks out at a measurable constant rate
The parent-to-daughter ratio in the closed mineral records elapsed half-lives
The parent isotope is replenished at a constant known rate
questions.why: Because the decay rate does not change, the ratio in a closed mineral is a clock that records elapsed time.

questions.stem: Which condition must hold for a radiometric date to be trustworthy?
options: The whole rock was metamorphosed after the mineral had formed
The rock sample contains several different radioactive isotopes of uranium
The mineral was heated well above its melting point later
The mineral stayed closed, losing no parent or daughter atoms
questions.why: An open system loses or gains parent or daughter and the ratio no longer records the original age.

questions.stem: A rock gives an age of 1.4 billion years with a 700-million-year isotope. What fraction of parent remains?
options: 25 percent, because two half-lives have elapsed
50 percent, because one half-life has elapsed
12.5 percent, because three half-lives have elapsed
6.25 percent, because four half-lives have elapsed
questions.why: 1.4 billion divided by 700 million is n = 2, so the parent has halved twice to 25 percent.
